items.prompt: What single habit do all mammals share, from a bat to a blue whale?

options.label: They nurse their young with milk
options.feedback: Every mammal has glands that make it, even the two species that hatch from eggs.

options.label: They give birth to live young
options.feedback: The platypus and the echidna are mammals too, and both hatch from an egg.

options.label: They have a visible tail
options.feedback: Apes and humans have lost theirs, and neither stops being a mammal.

options.label: They live only on land
options.feedback: Whales and dolphins spend their whole lives in water and never once touch land.

items.ok_line: Milk is the one thing no mammal goes without.
items.ko_line: Think of the one habit that has no exception, not even the egg-layers.
items.exp_text: The word mammal comes from the mammary gland, the organ that makes milk, and every species carries a pair. A mother's skin glands turn her own food into a fluid built for her newborn, and the young feeds on nothing else at first. Even the platypus and the echidna, which lay eggs instead of giving birth, still raise their hatchlings this way, the milk oozing through patches of skin because neither animal has a teat. Whatever else changes from one mammal to the next, that habit never does.

items.prompt: Why does a mammal's jaw work differently from a lizard's?

options.label: It is built from a single bone that hinges on the skull
options.feedback: One solid piece, moved by muscle, closing straight against the skull it hangs from.

options.label: It has no joint at all
options.feedback: A jaw with no joint could not open. Every mammal's jaw swings on one.

options.label: It is made of cartilage instead of bone
options.feedback: Cartilage flexes too easily to survive the force of a bite. A mammal jaw is solid bone.

options.label: It carries venom glands
options.feedback: Only a small number of mammals produce venom at all, and none delivers it through the jaw joint.

items.ok_line: One bone doing the whole job, hinged straight onto the skull.
items.ko_line: A reptile's jaw is built from several small bones stacked together. A mammal's is not.
items.exp_text: A lizard's lower jaw is a row of several bones bolted end to end, with the joint to the skull carried by one of the smaller ones near the back. In a mammal, all but one of those bones have vanished from the jaw, leaving a single piece called the dentary to do the whole job of biting, and it is this bone that hinges directly on the skull. The arrangement holds up to a much harder bite than the old multi-boned jaw ever could.

items.prompt: Where did the three tiny bones inside a mammal's ear come from?

options.label: Bones that once formed part of the jaw
options.feedback: Two bones that used to sit at the back of a reptile-like jaw were freed up and put to a new use.

options.label: Bones that grew new, just for hearing
options.feedback: Nothing in the ear was built from scratch. The bones already existed and simply changed job.

options.label: Bones from the roof of the mouth
options.feedback: The palate stayed exactly where it was. It contributed nothing to the middle ear.

options.label: Cartilage from the outer ear flap
options.feedback: The outer flap is soft tissue and stays outside the skull. The middle-ear bones are true bone, deep inside it.

items.ok_line: Old jaw hinges, repurposed as sound amplifiers.
items.ko_line: As the jaw shrank to one bone, the others did not disappear. They moved.
items.exp_title: A jaw hinge turned into an ear
items.exp_text: As the mammal jaw simplified down to a single bone, two small bones that used to sit at the back of a reptile-like jaw joint were left with no job to do. Rather than being lost, they migrated backward into the skull and settled beside a third bone already there, forming a tiny connected chain, the hammer, anvil and stirrup, that passes the vibration of sound from the eardrum inward. What began as part of a bite ended up sharpening a mammal's hearing.

items.prompt: Why does fur keep a mammal warm?

options.label: It traps a layer of still air against the skin
options.feedback: Trapped air barely moves, and still air carries heat away far more slowly than moving air does.

options.label: The hair itself produces heat
options.feedback: A hair is dead tissue once it has grown. It generates nothing on its own.

options.label: It reflects sunlight back outward
options.feedback: Reflecting light might matter on a bright day, but fur keeps an animal warm just as well at night or underground.

options.label: It thickens the skin underneath
options.feedback: Skin thickness barely changes with a fur coat. The warmth comes from what sits above the skin, not inside it.

items.ok_line: It is the trapped air doing the work, not the hair itself.
items.ko_line: A single hair conducts heat away almost as fast as bare skin would. Ask what sits between the hairs.
items.exp_title: A coat made mostly of air
items.exp_text: Each hair on its own does little to stop heat escaping, but thousands of them packed together trap a layer of air against the skin, and still air conducts heat away only slowly. A mammal can thicken that layer by fluffing its fur, drawing the hairs upright with tiny muscles to hold more air, or flatten it to release heat when it needs to cool down. The fur is really just scaffolding; the insulation is the air it holds still.

items.prompt: How does a mammal keep its body warm without depending on the sun or its surroundings?

options.label: Its own cells burn fuel constantly to release heat
options.feedback: Muscle and organ tissue keep working around the clock, and that work throws off heat as a by-product.

options.label: It stores heat absorbed during the day
options.feedback: A body cannot bank heat the way it banks fat. Without ongoing production, it cools within hours.

options.label: Its blood is naturally warmer than other animals'
options.feedback: Blood carries heat; it does not create it. Something in the body has to generate the warmth first.

options.label: Its skin blocks the surrounding temperature out entirely
options.feedback: No skin is a perfect seal. Heat still crosses it in both directions, warmth included.

items.ok_line: The heat comes from inside, made fresh, hour after hour.
items.ko_line: A lizard has fur-free skin and sunbathes to warm up. A mammal manages without either.
items.exp_title: Heat as a side effect of living
items.exp_text: Inside every mammal cell, fuel is broken down to power the ordinary business of living, moving, repairing, growing, and that breakdown releases heat as a by-product, the way a running engine grows warm whether or not warmth was the point. A mammal simply runs this process faster than an animal that relies on its surroundings, and fur or blubber then holds the heat in rather than letting it escape. The furnace is never switched off, which is why a mammal stays roughly the same temperature in a cold burrow as it does out in the sun.

items.prompt: Why does a mammal's mouth hold several different shapes of teeth?

options.label: Each shape is suited to a different part of the job of eating
options.feedback: A cutting edge, a piercing point and a grinding surface each solve a different problem.

options.label: Extra teeth grow in to replace worn ones nearby
options.feedback: Most mammals grow one adult set for life. New teeth do not sprout beside old ones to spell them.

options.label: Different shapes let the mouth close more tightly
options.feedback: A tight seal comes from the jaw muscles and joint, not from the outline of the teeth themselves.

options.label: It is left over from a much larger ancestral jaw
options.feedback: The variety is not a leftover. Each tooth shape is doing active work today.

items.ok_line: One tool for slicing, one for stabbing, one for crushing.
items.ko_line: A shark's mouth is full of teeth all the same shape. A mammal's is not, and that difference is the clue.
items.exp_title: A toolkit, not a row of spikes
items.exp_text: A reptile or a shark usually carries one tooth shape repeated down the jaw, replaced whenever it wears out, but a mammal instead grows several distinct shapes side by side and keeps them for life: chisel-edged incisors at the front for cutting, pointed canines behind them for piercing, and broad molars further back for crushing and grinding. Splitting the work this way lets a single mouth handle a much wider range of food than a row of identical teeth ever could.

items.prompt: What muscle does most of the work of pulling air into a mammal's lungs?

options.label: The diaphragm, a sheet of muscle below the lungs
options.feedback: It flattens downward, and the space above it opens up to pull air in.

options.label: The muscles of the throat, by swallowing air
options.feedback: Swallowing pushes food down the gullet, a completely separate tube from the airway.

options.label: The ribs alone, without any other muscle
options.feedback: The ribs do help, but on their own they widen the chest only slightly. Something below has to do more of the pulling.

options.label: The heart, by pumping blood into the lungs
options.feedback: The heart moves blood, not air. Blood and air travel through entirely separate systems inside the chest.

items.ok_line: A dome of muscle that flattens, and the lungs fill because of it.
items.ko_line: Reptiles get by on ribs alone. Mammals have something extra beneath the lungs that reptiles lack.
items.exp_title: A dome that flattens to make room
items.exp_text: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped sheet of muscle stretched beneath the lungs, sealing off the chest from the belly. When it contracts, it flattens and drops, and that sudden extra space inside the chest is exactly what the lungs expand to fill, drawing air in behind them. No reptile has one; a lizard has to rely on its ribs alone, which is one reason a mammal of the same size can sustain a far higher rate of breathing.

items.prompt: How does sweating cool a mammal down?

options.label: Evaporating moisture pulls heat away from the skin
options.feedback: Turning liquid into vapour takes energy, and that energy is drawn straight out of the skin as heat.

options.label: Sweat washes heat off the body like dirt
options.feedback: Heat is not a substance that rinses away. Cooling here works through a change of state, not a wash.

options.label: Sweat glands release cold fluid stored inside the body
options.feedback: Sweat starts out at body temperature. Nothing about it is cold when it reaches the skin.

options.label: Sweat thickens the skin to block outside heat
options.feedback: Sweat sits briefly on the surface and then evaporates. It changes nothing about the skin underneath.

items.ok_line: The cooling happens as the moisture turns to vapour, not before.
items.ko_line: Sweat feels warm the instant it appears on skin. The cooling comes a moment later, and only if it dries.
items.exp_text: A sweat gland pushes a thin film of fluid out onto the skin, and on its own that fluid would do nothing to cool anyone down. The cooling happens only when that moisture evaporates, because turning a liquid into vapour takes energy, and the only energy available nearby is the heat sitting in the skin. As the sweat dries, it carries that heat away with it, which is why sweating stops working well in damp air, where evaporation slows down.

items.prompt: What part of a mammal's brain is unusually large compared with a reptile's?

options.label: The neocortex, a folded outer layer
options.feedback: It is folded to pack a large surface into a small skull, and it handles complex processing.

options.label: The part that controls heartbeat
options.feedback: That structure sits deep in the brainstem, and it is not larger or more developed in mammals than in reptiles.

options.label: The part that controls eye colour
options.feedback: Eye colour is set by pigment cells in the eye itself. No brain region governs it at all.

options.label: The part that senses gravity
options.feedback: Balance is handled by the inner ear and a small region at the back of the brain, present in much the same form across many animals.

items.ok_line: A folded sheet of tissue that gives mammals room to think.
items.ko_line: Look for the region wrapped around the outside of the brain, not one buried deep inside it.
items.exp_title: A wrinkled sheet wrapped around the brain
items.exp_text: The neocortex is a layer of tissue that forms the outer surface of a mammal's brain, and in most mammals it is folded into ridges and grooves so that a much larger sheet of it can fit inside a skull of a given size. This is the tissue that handles complicated tasks: combining what different senses report, planning a movement before making it, learning from something that happened only once. A reptile's brain has nothing built quite like it, which is one reason mammal behaviour tends to be so much more flexible.

items.prompt: How does a placenta let most mammal young develop inside their mother rather than in an egg laid outside her body?

options.label: It links the mother's blood supply to the developing young
options.feedback: Nutrients and oxygen cross from her blood to the young's, and waste crosses back the other way.

options.label: It stores a large yolk for the young to feed on
options.feedback: A yolk is how an egg-laying animal supplies food. A placenta instead draws on the mother's own bloodstream while she is alive.

options.label: It seals the young inside a hard shell
options.feedback: A shell is exactly what most mammals do without. The placenta replaces the shell's job with a direct connection instead.

options.label: It pumps air directly into the young's lungs
options.feedback: Lungs stay unused until birth. Before that, oxygen reaches the young through blood, not through breathing.

items.ok_line: A living supply line, in place of a shell and a yolk.
items.ko_line: An egg carries its own food supply sealed inside it. A placenta works a different way entirely.
items.exp_title: A supply line instead of a shell
items.exp_text: In most mammals, an organ called the placenta grows against the wall of the mother's womb and threads her blood vessels close beside those of the developing young, close enough for nutrients, oxygen and waste to cross between the two without the bloods themselves ever mixing. This lets the young grow for weeks or months on a continuous supply rather than on a fixed store packed into an egg. The platypus and the echidna never evolved this link, which is exactly why they still lay eggs instead.
